products.overview: Map spectral information across materials, surfaces, and continuous processes with L-EOS™.
features: Scientific-Grade Hyperspectral Detection: Low background noise, high dynamic range, and high signal-to-noise performance for accurate SWIR material analysis.
Four-Stage Thermoelectric Cooling: Deep detector cooling down to −60 °C or −80 °C (model dependent) to minimize background noise and improve measurement quality.
Two SWIR Spectral Configurations: Available in L-EOS 1.7 (900–1700 nm) and L-EOS 2.5e (1000–2500 nm) to suit different hyperspectral imaging requirements.
512 Spatial Channels: Captures detailed spatial information for high-resolution line-scan hyperspectral imaging.
640 Spectral Channels: Acquires rich spectral data across the selected SWIR wavelength range.
15 µm Pixel Size: Delivers consistent image quality and precise hyperspectral data capture.
Industrial-Ready Architecture: Integrates infrared cameras, spectrometers, and telecentric optics into a robust industrial imaging platform.
Broad Application Support: Suitable for material sorting, recycling, food inspection, textile identification, mining, geology, core scanning, search and rescue, and UAV imaging.

technicalSpecs.label: Sensor
technicalSpecs.value: L-EOS 1.7: InGaAs — Alizé™ 1.7 or ZephIR™ 1.7 · L-EOS 2.5e: T2SL — ZephIR™ 2.5e

applications: Plastic Sorting: SWIR spectral information can support identification and separation of different plastic materials — L-EOS™ is listed by Photon etc. for plastic sorting and recycling applications, following a typical workflow of material stream → SWIR illumination → line scanning → hyperspectral data → material classification → sorting.

Textile Sorting & Recycling: SWIR hyperspectral imaging can help identify fabric types, blends, and material composition — Photon etc. specifically presents L-EOS™ for next-generation fabric identification, highlighting its use in distinguishing complex blends and compositions.

Food Quality & Safety: Spectral imaging can support non-destructive material and quality assessment workflows, covering product inspection, material differentiation, quality assessment, spectral classification, and non-destructive analysis.

Mining & Geology: Hyperspectral information can be used to map and distinguish geological or mineralogical features, supporting workflows where material differences need to be mapped and characterized.
Core Scanning: Line-based hyperspectral imaging can support continuous analysis of geological core samples — Photon etc. lists core scanning among the L-EOS™ application resources.
Search & Rescue: Infrared spectral imaging can provide information beyond conventional visible imaging.
UAV Imaging: SWIR imaging can be integrated into aerial inspection and remote sensing workflows.
Material Characterization: Spectral signatures can support differentiation of materials.
Industrial Recycling: Hyperspectral identification can support automated material classification workflows.

faqs.question: What is L-EOS™?
faqs.answer: L-EOS™ is a hyperspectral SWIR imaging system from Photon etc. designed for industrial infrared imaging, material analysis, sorting, recycling, textiles, geology, food applications, and other hyperspectral workflows.

faqs.question: What type of camera is L-EOS™?
faqs.answer: L-EOS™ is a hyperspectral linescan camera system designed for industrial SWIR imaging applications.

faqs.question: What wavelength range does L-EOS™ cover?
faqs.answer: L-EOS™ is available in two configurations. L-EOS 1.7 covers 900–1700 nm, while L-EOS 2.5e covers 1000–2500 nm.

faqs.question: What is the difference between L-EOS 1.7 and L-EOS 2.5e?
faqs.answer: L-EOS 1.7 uses an InGaAs sensor and covers 900–1700 nm. L-EOS 2.5e uses a T2SL sensor and covers 1000–2500 nm. They also differ in spectral resolution and spectral sampling.

faqs.question: What sensor does L-EOS 1.7 use?
faqs.answer: L-EOS 1.7 uses an InGaAs sensor, with Alizé™ 1.7 or ZephIR™ 1.7 sensor options listed by Photon etc.

faqs.question: What sensor does L-EOS 2.5e use?
faqs.answer: L-EOS 2.5e uses a T2SL sensor, specifically the ZephIR™ 2.5e configuration listed by Photon etc.

faqs.question: How many spatial channels does L-EOS™ have?
faqs.answer: Both L-EOS configurations provide 512 spatial channels.

faqs.question: How many spectral channels does L-EOS™ have?
faqs.answer: Both L-EOS configurations provide 640 spectral channels.

faqs.question: What is the spectral resolution of L-EOS 1.7?
faqs.answer: L-EOS 1.7 has a spectral resolution of 7.8 nm.

faqs.question: What is the spectral resolution of L-EOS 2.5e?
faqs.answer: L-EOS 2.5e has a spectral resolution of 15.3 nm.

faqs.question: What is the spectral sampling of L-EOS 1.7?
faqs.answer: The typical spectral sampling of L-EOS 1.7 is 1.3 nm/px.

faqs.question: What is the spectral sampling of L-EOS 2.5e?
faqs.answer: The typical spectral sampling of L-EOS 2.5e is 2.6 nm/px.

faqs.question: What is the pixel size of L-EOS™?
faqs.answer: Both L-EOS configurations have a 15 µm pixel size.

faqs.question: Does L-EOS™ use thermoelectric cooling?
faqs.answer: Yes. L-EOS™ uses four stages of thermoelectric cooling.

faqs.question: How cold can the L-EOS™ detector get?
faqs.answer: At 20°C ambient temperature, L-EOS 1.7 can reach -60°C or -80°C, while L-EOS 2.5e can reach -80°C.

faqs.question: What is L-EOS™ used for?
faqs.answer: L-EOS™ is used for industrial hyperspectral imaging applications including material sorting, plastic sorting, textile analysis and recycling, food quality and safety, mining and geology, core scanning, search and rescue, and UAV applications.

faqs.question: Can L-EOS™ be used for textile analysis?
faqs.answer: Yes. Photon etc. specifically presents L-EOS™ for textile analysis and fabric identification, including applications involving complex blends and recycling.

faqs.question: Can L-EOS™ be used for plastic sorting?
faqs.answer: Yes. Plastic sorting is listed by Photon etc. as an application for L-EOS™.

faqs.question: Can L-EOS™ be used for mining and geology?
faqs.answer: Yes. Photon etc. lists mining and geology among the industrial applications for its hyperspectral imaging solutions and provides core-scanning resources associated with L-EOS™.

faqs.question: Can L-EOS™ be used for food quality and safety?
faqs.answer: Yes. Food Quality / Safety is listed among the L-EOS™ application resources.

faqs.question: Can L-EOS™ be used with UAVs?
faqs.answer: UAV is listed among the L-EOS™ application resources. The complete UAV configuration should be evaluated according to the imaging platform and application requirements.

faqs.question: Is L-EOS™ suitable for continuous industrial processes?
faqs.answer: L-EOS™ belongs to Photon etc.'s Linescan Cameras category, which is designed for high-throughput industrial sorting and continuous-flow analysis.

longForm.heroHook: Long-Lifetime Hyperspectral SWIR Imaging for Industrial Material Analysis
longForm.heroLead: Map spectral information across materials, surfaces, and continuous processes with L-EOS™. Photon etc. L-EOS™ is a hyperspectral SWIR imaging system designed for industrial applications that require spatial and spectral information from materials and processes. It combines a scientific-grade infrared camera, thermoelectric cooling, spectrometer technology, and an industrial-ready design for demanding imaging workflows. L-EOS™ is available in two configurations covering different SWIR spectral regions: L-EOS 1.7 covering 900–1700 nm, and L-EOS 2.5e covering 1000–2500 nm. Both configurations provide 512 spatial channels and 640 spectral channels, with 6-pixel spatial resolution and 15 µm pixel size. The L-EOS 1.7 configuration uses an InGaAs sensor, while L-EOS 2.5e uses a T2SL sensor. Four-stage thermoelectric cooling can reach temperatures as low as -60°C or -80°C, depending on the configuration. Cooling helps reduce background noise and support high signal-to-noise performance during infrared imaging. L-EOS™ is suited to industrial workflows including material sorting, textile identification, recycling, food quality and safety, mining and geology, core scanning, search and rescue, and UAV-based applications.

sections.title: Why SWIR Hyperspectral Imaging Matters
body: A conventional image primarily records spatial information. Hyperspectral imaging adds another layer: spectral information at each measured spatial position. For industrial applications, this can be valuable when two materials look similar in visible light but exhibit different spectral responses in the SWIR region.

L-EOS™ combines line-based spatial acquisition with multiple spectral channels, creating a hyperspectral measurement that can be used to investigate material differences across a scene — spatial + spectral information in place of appearance-only imaging, spectral-response-based discrimination in place of limited spectral discrimination, and spectral-data-based classification in place of image-based classification.

Short-wave infrared imaging can provide spectral information outside the visible range, which is useful for industrial applications where material differences are difficult to identify from visible appearance alone. L-EOS™ extends spectral imaging into SWIR through its two configurations — 900–1700 nm with L-EOS 1.7 and 1000–2500 nm with L-EOS 2.5e — with the appropriate spectral range depending on the material and the spectral features that need to be measured.
sections.disclaimer: If the objective is material identification, share the materials being differentiated, the expected spectral range, the imaging distance, and whether the workflow is continuous or stationary. This helps determine whether the L-EOS 1.7 or L-EOS 2.5e configuration is more appropriate.

sections.title: Thermoelectric Cooling and Signal Quality
sections.description: Infrared detectors can be affected by background signal and thermal effects. L-EOS™ addresses this through a four-stage thermoelectric cooling architecture. Photon etc. specifies operating temperatures as low as -60°C or -80°C for L-EOS 1.7, and -80°C for L-EOS 2.5e, with these values specified at 20°C ambient temperature. The cooling architecture is intended to support the low-background and high signal-to-noise characteristics of the system.
